Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Did computers write poetry before chatbots existed? The first attempt is older than the computer itself, and one famous “machine poem” was a joke that people took seriously. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • OpenAI dissolves its separate robotics team: its general-purpose AI, it says, can now run robots directly. OpenAI has dissolved its separate robotics team and moved its people into other groups. The company says this is no retreat: its general-purpose AI model, the kind that answers questions and writes programs, turned out to be able to control robots directly, so a purpose-built robot “brain” may not be needed. The evidence is thin so far: the main test ran in a computer simulation, and in one trial with real robot arms the model fully completed only 7 tasks out of 100. OpenAI is also losing money and cutting side projects. Read more and the background.
  • The opposite bet: Runway gives away an AI built specially for robots, trained mostly by watching video. The company Runway has made the opposite bet and released, free for anyone to download, an AI built specially for robots. It learned mostly from ordinary video: it first “imagines” what should happen in the next second or so and then works out the arm movements. On a real robot arm it succeeded in 88 of 100 simple attempts, such as putting a banana on a plate, but it confuses similar objects and cannot plan a long task by itself. Nearly all the tests were run by Runway itself. Read more and the background.
  • Google’s newest model tops an independent maths test; the three leaders are nearly level, but their prices are not. On an independent test of mathematical ability run by universities in Switzerland and Bulgaria, Google’s new model has taken first place with 85%, ahead of Anthropic’s Claude (83%) and OpenAI’s model (81%). The gaps are within the test’s own margin of error, so really the three are close together. The prices are not: one attempt at one problem costs about $1 with OpenAI’s model, $16 with Google’s and $40 with Anthropic’s. The Claude model in the table is the one writing this email. Read more and the background.
  • After the Nvidia chief’s exit: a petition to bring him back, and Asian governments check on their chip supplies. After Jensen Huang, the long-time head of the chip maker Nvidia, resigned on Thursday, more than 115,000 people have signed a petition asking the board to bring him back while an investigation runs; the signers are said to include thousands of Nvidia employees, and Elon Musk. Governments in Asia are checking on their supplies: South Korea says Nvidia has reaffirmed a delivery of 260,000 AI chips, while Taiwan and Japan are urging calm. Almost all the world’s AI runs on Nvidia’s chips, which is why this matters. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Days before Anthropic’s share sale: its chief calls buying computers the company’s “deepest dilemma”, and a former employee calls for a pause, IBM tries a new defence against a known weakness: AI that obeys instructions hidden in a document.

Answer to the question of the day. Yes, and for a surprisingly long time, as the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok tells it in a chapter from a book by the philologist Boris Orekhov. As early as 1845 an Englishman, John Clark, showed a mechanical device called Eureka that put together lines of Latin verse, about one a minute; the newspapers found it useless but amusing. In 1956 an American journal printed a humorous story about an invented professor and his verse-writing machine. Its deliberately nonsensical lines reached Soviet specialists without the story around them, were tidied up by a poet into something that made sense, and were quoted for years as a real machine poem, at a time when computers wrote no verse at all. The first real experiment came in 1959: the German mathematician Theo Lutz had a computer pick words at random from the vocabulary of Kafka’s novel “The Castle” and fit them into simple sentences. In 1961 another German limited the vocabulary to Christmas words and got verses that were quite readable, though without rhyme. All these early programs did one of two things: they shuffled the words or phrases of an existing text, or they filled ready-made sentence patterns with random words from a list. The machine understood nothing; it was, in the author’s image, rolling dice. A third method came later: the program first “reads” a text, counts how often one word follows another and continues by the odds. The word suggestions on your phone’s keyboard work on that principle today. Sistemny Blok, “The muse with punch cards: how computers learned to write verse half a century before neural networks” (July 2026) (article in Russian).
